summary: Clarks Point Light, New Bedford: a merchants' beacon of 1797, a stone tower of 1804 and, from 1869, a light on Fort Taber; discontinued 1898, relit 2001, inactive since 2016.

light.note: A wooden beacon built by local merchants in 1797 burned about a year later (LighthouseFriends). Its replacement was first lit 12 October 1799 (LighthouseFriends). The record's 1804 is the stone tower.

lens.note: A fifth-order Fresnel lens was installed in 1856 (LighthouseFriends). The sources read do not describe the lens in use today.

structures.note: Burned about a year after building, in a severe thunderstorm (Ricketson; LighthouseFriends).
38 ft (11.6 m) tall. Raised 4 ft (1.2 m) with a new octagonal iron lantern in 1818 (New England Lighthouses). Demolished 1906.

structures.type: rectangular wooden tower on Fort Taber
structures.note: Built on the fort's northerly tower to take the lantern from the stone tower. 68 ft (21 m) above the sea (New England Lighthouses). Restored 1997-2001.

access.note: Grounds open. The lighthouse and Fort Taber are closed (LighthouseFriends visitor information).

events.note: Local merchants build a wooden beacon on Clark's Point (LighthouseFriends; Ricketson).
The wooden beacon burns about a year after it was built, in a severe thunderstorm at night (Ricketson; LighthouseFriends).
A plot at the end of the point deeded for the light on 16 June 1800; on 29 July 1800 Congress accepts financial responsibility for the beacon and agrees to appoint a keeper (LighthouseFriends).
Octagonal rubblestone tower, 38 ft (11.6 m) tall, completed; Congress committed $2,500 on 16 March 1804 (New England Lighthouses; LighthouseFriends).
Fixed white light with a focal plane of 50 ft (LighthouseFriends). No date beyond the year is given.
Tower raised 4 ft with a new octagonal iron lantern (New England Lighthouses).
Old-style lantern room replaced with one of larger panes (LighthouseFriends).
Lantern and apparatus moved to a new rectangular wooden tower on Fort Taber; first shown from there 15 June 1869, 68 ft above the sea (New England Lighthouses; LighthouseFriends; USCG 2001 article).
Light extinguished 30 April 1898, after Butler Flats Light was completed (LighthouseFriends; New England Lighthouses).
Old stone tower demolished (LighthouseFriends; New England Lighthouses; USCG 2001 article).
Clarks Point Light and Fort Taber designated a National Register district (USCG 2001 article).
Briefly relit for the bicentennial, then vandalised and darkened again (USCG 2001 article).
Vandals burned and nearly destroyed the light after its early 1970s renovation (LighthouseFriends; the year is the bicentennial relighting, after which vandalism is reported).
City of New Bedford begins restoration and commits $7 million to renovating the light and building a park at the fort (USCG 2001 article).
Relit 15 June 2001, the 132nd anniversary of its first lighting (LighthouseFriends).

corrections.proposed: wooden beacon built 1797 (burned about a year later); octagonal rubblestone tower built 1804 (demolished 1906); rectangular wooden tower on Fort Taber built 1869 (standing)
corrections.why: The 1797 beacon was of wood, and the stone tower dates from 1804 and was demolished in 1906. The tower standing today is the 1869 wooden structure on Fort Taber.

1804 is the stone tower's date. A wooden beacon was built in 1797 and burned about a year later, and its replacement was first lit 12 October 1799 (LighthouseFriends). Proposed 1799 as the first dated lighting; the editor may prefer the 1797 beacon.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record gives 1804, the stone tower's year. The station's light is older: the merchants' 1797 beacon burned about a year later, and a replacement was first lit on 12 October 1799 (LighthouseFriends). The 1804 date is kept only as the stone tower's build date.

notes_for_editor: 1) Record structure: 'tower, stone, built 1797, standing' is wrong on three counts (see corrections). The 1797 beacon was wooden, the stone tower dates from 1804 and was demolished in 1906, and the standing tower is the 1869 wooden tower on Fort Taber. 2) Record first_lit 1804 and the Rowlett 1804 event: the station's light is older (1797 beacon; replacement first lit 12 October 1799). Proposed 1799 in corrections. 3) NRHP 73001954 is the Fort Taber district nomination (the fort at Clark's Point), not a lighthouse nomination. The form's OCR is letter-spaced and its text has no lighthouse entry (grep for 'light', 'lantern', 'beacon', 'tower' finds nothing), so it could not be quoted and was not used for the lighthouse. The fort's purchase year differs: LighthouseFriends gives 24 September 1857; the nomination's OCR appears to give 1858 for the purchase and May 1861 for the start of construction, but these could not be quoted cleanly, so the story says 'late 1850s'. 4) Wikipedia (lead only, not cited) gives 'Automated 2001' and says the Coast Guard rescinded the private aid licence in 2015; LighthouseFriends says inactive since 2016. Unresolved; check the current Coast Guard List of Lights. 5) USCG Historian's page (history.uscg.mil, Clarks Point Light): a search snippet gives 'Station Established: 1797', 'First Lit: 1869', 'Automated: Yes - 2001' and 'Operational: Yes', which conflicts with LighthouseFriends's 'inactive'. The page itself was blocked (403) and was not read. 6) The Ricketson chowder story (raising of the wooden beacon, Ricketson p. 80) conflicts with LighthouseFriends (raising of the 1804 stone tower's frame). The story gives both. 7) Keepers: the roster prints David Wilber as 1815-1919 (LighthouseFriends: 1815 to 1819); LighthouseFriends's list has Joseph Howland (1803-1813), missing from the roster; the New England Lighthouses history calls the Howland successor 'Edward W.' (roster and LighthouseFriends 'Edward H.') and gives Henry M. Smith to 1873 (roster 1872). The Bulletin's 1872-1879 for Amos C. Baker, Sr., and its death year 1879, conflict with the roster (1873-1880) and LighthouseFriends's death date (7 January 1881). 8) Not used: LighthouseFriends's account of an enslaved woman and her two children being brought to the light in the 1850s by a supply vessel. The page gives no source for it, and nothing read corroborates it. The editor should check it before anything is published. 9) The Lighthouse Board volume labelled 1895 (annualreportlig00boargoog) is the report for the fiscal year ended 30 June 1895; the Butler Flat passage is cited without a printed page because the local copy has no page index. 10) The 1892 entry (136) is cited to the fiscal 1892 report from its position in the bound volume (scan page 391). Its printed page is not confirmed: the OCR index did not show a Clark Point entry, so the story gives the scan page only; the report's year is inferred, not read from its title page. 11) Ricketson's 1858 history is cited to the djvu text; the printed page (80) is from the book's own index entry 'Clark's Point light-house, 80' and the page marker before the passage. 12) The 1929 Bulletin's family statement names the father's keepership as 1872 to 1879; no other source read agrees with those years. 13) The 2001 Coast Guard article's author is Seaman Amy Thomas, First District. 14) Staffing and the current lens are not described in the sources read, so they are left out of the facts. 15) The 1976 damage event is dated to the year of the bicentennial relighting because the article puts the vandalism after it; LighthouseFriends puts the burning after the early 1970s renovation. Year approximate. 16) The 1798 burning year is approximate ('about a year' after 1797, LighthouseFriends). 17) Fact-check pass 2026-10-27: each footnoted sentence was checked against LighthouseFriends, the New England Lighthouses history, the USLHS roster, the Light-House Board volumes (1892, 1895), the 1929 Bulletin, the 2001 Coast Guard article and Ricketson (1858, djvu text). Ricketson's p. 80 is confirmed by the book's own page markers: the passage sits between the markers for pages 80 and 81, and the markers are page headers (Chapter VIII starts on p. 78 in the contents, and the '78' marker comes just before its heading). Changes made to the story: the roster is attributed to the U.S. Lighthouse Society archive; 'Fort Taber' is now described as an unofficial name (LighthouseFriends: the Army never recognized it); the Carpender quotation now reads 'some of the others', as the 1838 report and LighthouseFriends give it, not 'some of the lamps'; the New England Lighthouses 52-foot height for the 1804 light is stated against LighthouseFriends' 50 feet; the New England Lighthouses keeper list (Smith 1843-1873) is stated against the roster (1843-1872); the 1857 purchase date is taken from LighthouseFriends; the sentence 'the merchants did not keep the light for long' is removed; the 1892 Light-House Board entry is cited by scan page 391 because its printed page could not be confirmed (the story and the first draft of this record gave p. 56, which the OCR head does not confirm); Ricketson's 'burnt' is used for 'destroyed'; the 1997 restoration is worded as LighthouseFriends and the 2001 article give it. Still unverified: the printed page of the FY1892 entry, the printed page of the FY1895 Butler Flat entry, the NRHP district nomination (NRHP 73001954 OCR, see note 3), the current Light List characteristic.
